summary: Defines U-NAPTR, a Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service application that maps a domain name to a URI for a particular application service or protocol. It extends the earlier straightforward NAPTR (S-NAPTR) approach, so clients can use DNS to find where a service for a domain actually lives. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: U-NAPTR lets a DNS NAPTR record point at a URI instead of at another domain name. A client asks DNS for the service of a domain and gets back a URI such as prota://someisp.example.com, which it then resolves. It is a small extension of S-NAPTR that adds the U flag and one tightly limited regular expression form.

questions: how to map a domain to a uri using dns
what is the u flag in naptr
subtitle: A small extension to S-NAPTR that lets a DNS record point straight at a URI for a domain's service.

tldr.problem: S-NAPTR finds services for a domain without regular expressions, but that rule also rules out returning a URI. Several applications found this too limiting.
tldr.mechanism: U-NAPTR adds a "U" flag and a tightly limited regular expression of the form !.*!URI! so that a NAPTR record can hand back a constant URI.
tldr.outcome: Clients can map a domain to a URI for an application service without implementing full regular expressions. The RFC is a Proposed Standard from April 2007.

today: RFC 4848 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is still the definition of the URI-enabled NAPTR application.

sections.title: Why a Domain-to-URI Lookup Is Needed
sections.content:
The purpose of this document is to define a new, straightforward Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service (DDDS) application that allows mapping of domain names to URIs for particular application services and protocols. That makes it possible to look up which services are available for a given domain.

Although it defines a new and separate DDDS application, called U-NAPTR, it is built from the same principles as the Straightforward NAPTR (S-NAPTR) application specified in RFC 3958. The document is not an update of S-NAPTR, but it points the reader at that document for extensive coverage of motivation and implementation considerations.

S-NAPTR provides application service location that does not rely on rigid domain naming conventions. It is called straightforward in part because it rules out the use of regular expressions in NAPTR records. That rule also rules out the possibility of providing a URI as the target of the resolution. A number of applications, some specified and some proposed, find the restriction too limiting, which makes S-NAPTR a near miss for their needs.

U-NAPTR is therefore a modest extension to S-NAPTR that accommodates URIs as targets, without allowing the full range of possible regular expressions in NAPTR records. Its intention is to provide everything S-NAPTR does, except that it allows the "U" flag in the NAPTR record and one specific form of regular expression.
sections.plainLanguage: S-NAPTR lets a client find the service of a domain without depending on naming conventions, but it forbids regular expressions in NAPTR records, and that also forbids returning a URI. This document relaxes the rule just enough to allow a URI as the answer, and no more.

sections.title: Permitted Flags
sections.content:
U-NAPTR permits the same flags as S-NAPTR, which are "S", "A" or empty, plus the "U" flag.

For this application, the presence of the "U" flag in the NAPTR record indicates that the REGEXP field must be populated, and consequently that the REPLACEMENT field is empty. The regular expression in the REGEXP field must be of the limited form described in the next section, and the result of evaluating it is the URI that results from the resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAPTR record carries a flag that says what to do with its output. U-NAPTR keeps the flags S, A and empty, and adds U. The U flag means the record carries a regular expression whose result is the URI to use.

sections.title: The Permitted Regular Expression
sections.content:
U-NAPTR permits regular expressions of a form that replaces the matched string completely with a URI, expressed as a constant string:

u-naptr-regexp = "!.*!"<URI>"!"

where <URI> is as defined in STD 66, the URI syntax specification in RFC 3986.

The document calls this essentially a dodge around the fact that the REPLACEMENT field in NAPTR is required to produce only a fully qualified domain name, and therefore cannot be used for a URI. With this limited form of regular expression, applications using U-NAPTR need not implement full regular expression parsers.
sections.plainLanguage: The only regular expression a U-NAPTR record may hold replaces the whole matched text with a constant URI, written as an exclamation mark, the text, an exclamation mark and the URI. An application using this does not need a general regular expression parser.

sections.title: Sample U-NAPTR DNS Records
sections.content:
The sample NAPTR resource records for example.com show four entries. "WP" is the imagined application service tag for white pages, and "EM" is the application service tag for an imagined Extensible Messaging application service.

The first record has order 100 and preference 10, an empty flag string, the service WP:whois++, an empty regular expression and the replacement bunyip.example.com.. The second has order 100 and preference 20, the flag "s", the service WP:ldap, an empty regular expression and the replacement _ldap._tcp.myldap.example.com.. The third has order 200 and preference 10, the flag "u", the service EM:protA, the regular expression !.*!prota://someisp.example.com! and an empty replacement. The fourth has order 200 and preference 30, the flag "a", the service EM:protB, an empty regular expression and the replacement myprotB.example.com..

The third record is the one that returns a URI: the flag says the regular expression must be there, and evaluating the regular expression yields the URI that the client then resolves.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show four NAPTR records for one domain: two ordinary S-NAPTR style records and two that use the new flag, one of which returns a URI directly.

sections.title: Formal Definition: Keys, Rules, Outputs and the Database
sections.content:
The document formally defines the DDDS application. The Application Unique String is a fully qualified domain name for which an authoritative server for a particular service is sought. The First Well Known Rule is the identity rule, meaning that the output of the rule is the Application Unique String itself. The Expected Output is the information necessary to connect to authoritative servers, that is a host, a port, a protocol or a URI, for an application service within a given domain.

This application uses only three of the flags defined for the URI/URN resolution application: "S", "A" and "U". No other flags are valid. If a client obtains a NAPTR record for a U-NAPTR application that contains any other flag, that record should be ignored and processing continues with the next record, if any.

These flags are for terminal lookups, which means that the rule is the last one and the flag determines what the next stage should be. The "S" flag means the output of the rule is a fully qualified domain name for which one or more SRV records exist. The "A" flag means the output is a domain name and should be used to look up address records for that domain. The "U" flag means the output is a URI that should be resolved to obtain access to the described service. If the flag string is empty, the next lookup is for another NAPTR record, for the replacement target.

At present only one DDDS database is specified for this application. RFC 3403 specifies a database that uses the NAPTR DNS resource record to contain the rewrite rules, with the keys for this database encoded as domain names. The First Well Known Rule produces a domain name, and that domain name is the key used for the first lookup: the NAPTR records for that domain are requested.

DNS servers MAY interpret flag values and use that information to include appropriate NAPTR, SRV or A records in the Additional Information portion of the DNS packet. Clients are encouraged to check for additional information but are not required to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines the lookup formally. The key is the domain name being looked up, the first rule does nothing, and the expected output is the host, port, protocol or URI needed to reach the service. Only three flags are valid, and a record with any other flag is skipped. The lookup asks DNS for the NAPTR records of that domain.

sections.title: Service Parameters and Valid Rules
sections.content:
The Service Parameters for this application are a string of characters that follows this syntax:

service-parms = [ [app-service] *(":" app-protocol)]
app-service   = experimental-service  / iana-registered-service
app-protocol  = experimental-protocol / iana-registered-protocol
experimental-service      = "x-" 1*30ALPHANUMSYM
experimental-protocol     = "x-" 1*30ALPHANUMSYM
iana-registered-service   = ALPHA *31ALPHANUMSYM
iana-registered-protocol  = ALPHA *31ALPHANUMSYM
ALPHA         =  %x41-5A / %x61-7A   ; A-Z / a-z
DIGIT         =  %x30-39 ; 0-9
SYM           =  %x2B / %x2D / %x2E  ; "+" / "-" / "."
ALPHANUMSYM   =  ALPHA / DIGIT / SYM

The service parameters may consist of an empty string, just an application service, or an application service with one or more application protocol specifications separated by the colon symbol. The application service must be an IANA-registered service, and the protocol identifiers valid for the application protocol are standard, registered protocols.

The syntax is similar to, but not the same as, the one used in the URI DDDS application, and it is expanded to allow the characters that are valid in any URI scheme name. Because the plus sign, which is the separator used in the RFC 3404 service parameter string, is allowed in URI scheme names, the colon is chosen as the separator here. The tags are limited to 32 characters, must start with an alphabetic character, and the service parameters are case-insensitive.

The permitted rules are substitution rules and regular expressions of the same limited syntax as before, that is a regular expression that replaces the domain name with a URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The service field names the application service and, after a colon, the protocols that may serve it. Tags starting with x- are experimental and may be reused by anyone; other tags are registered with IANA. The separator is a colon because the plus sign used elsewhere is allowed in URI scheme names.

sections.title: Registering Service and Protocol Tags
sections.content:
The document places no requirements on IANA itself, but it provides the basis on which U-NAPTR-using services can use the existing IANA registries for application service tags and application protocol tags, defined in RFC 3958.

As with S-NAPTR, all application service and protocol tags that start with "x-" are considered experimental, and no provision is made to prevent duplicate use of the same string. The document says to use them at your own risk. All other tags are registered on the "specification required" option, with the further stipulation that the specification is an RFC of any category.

There are no further restrictions on the tags beyond the syntax defined in the document. The defining RFC must clearly identify and describe, for each tag being registered: the application protocol or service tag, the intended usage, the interoperability considerations, the security considerations, and any relevant related publications. It may also include further application-specific restrictions, such as limitations on the types of URIs that may be returned for the application service.
sections.plainLanguage: New service and protocol tags are registered the same way as for S-NAPTR. The defining RFC has to say what the tag is, what it is for, how implementations interoperate, what the security consequences are, and any related publications.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
U-NAPTR has the same security considerations as S-NAPTR. It has one additional consideration: resolving the URI obtained from the resolution has its own security implications, covered in the URI specification.

In essence, using DNSSEC, client software can be confident that the URI obtained with U-NAPTR is indeed the one specified by the administrator of the domain from which it was retrieved. The validity of the service reached by resolving that URI is a separate matter, and is handled by the security practices of URI resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: U-NAPTR has the same security considerations as S-NAPTR, plus the ones that come with resolving a URI. With DNSSEC a client can trust that the URI came from the domain owner, but whether the service behind the URI is the right one is a matter of how the URI is resolved.

viz.caption: THE FLAGS A U-NAPTR RECORD MAY CARRY

items.label: SRV
items.desc: The output is a domain name for which SRV records exist.

items.label: Address
items.desc: The output is a domain name to look up address records for.

items.label: URI
items.desc: The output is a URI that must be resolved to reach the service.

items.label: Another NAPTR
items.desc: The next lookup is for another NAPTR record, the replacement target.

viz.caption: THE ONE REGULAR EXPRESSION FORM U-NAPTR ALLOWS
SAMPLE NAPTR RECORDS FOR EXAMPLE.COM FROM RFC 4848, SECTION 3

data.title: Sample records
data.code:
example.com.
;;       order pref flags
IN NAPTR 100   10   ""    "WP:whois++"      ( ; service
                          ""                  ; regexp
                          bunyip.example.com. ; replacement
                                            )
IN NAPTR 100   20   "s"   "WP:ldap"         ( ; service
                          ""                  ; regexp
                         _ldap._tcp.myldap.example.com. ; replacement
                                            )
IN NAPTR 200   10   "u"    "EM:protA"        ( ; service
                          "!.*!prota://someisp.example.com!" ; regexp
                          ""                  ; replacement
                                            )
IN NAPTR 200   30   "a"   "EM:protB"          ; service
                          ""                  ; regexp
                          myprotB.example.com.; replacement
                                            )
